title: Site-specific microRNA responses in lungs of pigs depend on the host-adaptation of H1N1 influenza A virus

analysis.research_question_and_background: Cross-species transmission of influenza A virus (IAV) represents a major risk for emergence of new pandemics, however, the host molecular responses invoked by cross-species IAV infection remain incompletely defined.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Notably, extensive downregulation of miRNAs in the lower lungs after huH1N1 infection coincided with robust ISG induction, despite huH1N1 viral lung load being comparable to swH1N1 viral load.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The swine-adapted IAV, in contrast, triggered stronger RIG-I-like receptor and cGAS transcription without substantial miRNA changes.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the host molecular responses to influenza A virus (IAV) in pigs, focusing on the differences in pulmonary miRNA expression between human-adapted (huH1N1) and swine-adapted (swH1N1) IAV strains. These findings suggest that miRNA-mediated antiviral signaling may play a role in shaping the outcome of IAV infection depending on the degree of host adaptation. The study contributes to understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying cross-species IAV transmission and may inform future research on viral host adaptation and immune responses.

title: Age and seasonal patterns of respiratory pathogens and their codetections revealed by multiplex PCR

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the age and seasonal patterns of respiratory pathogens, particularly influenza viruses, and their co-detections in a post-pandemic setting, as RTIs remain a significant public health issue due to their diverse etiologies and overlapping clinical presentations.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective cross-sectional study analyzed consecutive nasopharyngeal swab specimens from patients with clinically suspected RTIs at Siirt Training and Research Hospital in Türkiye between January 2024 and December 2025. analysis.methods: The study used multiplex RT-qPCR to detect respiratory pathogens and performed multivariable logistic regression analysis to identify independent factors associated with pathogen detection, including age and season.
analysis.main_results: Among 1,666 specimens, respiratory pathogens were detected in 1,166 (70.0%). Bacterial-only detection accounted for 473 (40.6%), viral-only detection for 395 (33.9%), and viral–bacterial co-detection for 298 (25.6%) of positive specimens. Children had significantly higher odds of pathogen detection than adults (aOR 2.27, 95% CI 1.72–2.99; p < 0.001). Respiratory pathogen detection was significantly lower during summer (aOR 0.58, 95% CI 0.43–0.78; p < 0.001) and autumn (aOR 0.57, 95% CI 0.43–0.75; p < 0.001) compared to winter.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate distinct age-related and seasonal patterns in respiratory pathogen detection, including frequent viral–bacterial co-detection, which provides a more comprehensive understanding of the epidemiology of these pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results can inform improved surveillance strategies, enhance diagnostic approaches, and guide targeted public health interventions to address seasonal variations and age-specific risks in respiratory infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's retrospective design and reliance on anonymized data may limit the depth of clinical interpretation, and the evidence is moderate due to the absence of prospective data and potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the age and seasonal patterns of respiratory pathogens, particularly influenza viruses, and their co-detections in a post-pandemic setting using multiplex RT-qPCR. title: Beyond Viral Load: A Mechanistic Model of Virus-Immune Dynamics and Age-Dependent Influenza Severity

It highlights a knowledge gap in understanding how immune responses mechanistically drive symptom severity beyond viral replication.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The authors developed an integrative within-host modeling framework that links infection dynamics, immune responses, and symptom progression. The study used murine influenza data to quantify host weight loss as a measure of symptom severity.
analysis.methods: The framework incorporated key immune components and a mechanistic representation of symptom progression, with inflammatory signaling—particularly TNF-mediated pathways—identified as central to linking immune activity to symptom severity. The model explicitly connected viral replication, immune responses, and clinical symptoms through a unified dynamical system.
analysis.main_results: The analysis showed that inflammatory signaling, especially TNF-mediated pathways, drives the coupling between immune activity and symptom severity. Aged hosts exhibited prolonged inflammatory responses that amplified and sustained symptom burden despite comparable viral kinetics.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as demonstrating that disease severity cannot be inferred from viral load alone but instead emerges from the dynamic interplay between immune regulation and host physiology. The novelty lies in explicitly connecting immune-mediated pathology to symptom manifestation through a mechanistic model.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The framework provides a quantitative basis for understanding age-specific morbidity in influenza and suggests that interventions targeting immune-mediated pathology, rather than viral replication, may be more effective for reducing disease severity.

analysis.summary_en: This study develops an integrative within-host modeling framework to mechanistically link influenza infection dynamics, immune responses, and symptom severity.
